summary: AE + SE demo focused on extreme edge cases: long context windows, sustained high TPS, streaming with backpressure and timeouts. Demo showed API behaviors, console telemetry, Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization, and fallback/retry strategies. Customer requested benchmarks, POC, and security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Liam O'Connor: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Liam from Redwood, AE, with Priya our solutions engineer. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Nina Park: Nina here, CTO, DataScale.
[00:08] Carlos Rivera: Carlos, ML Eng.
[00:10] Samir Patel: Samir, infra.
[00:12] Priya Gupta: Hi all, Priya here, SE at Redwood. We'll walk through a demo that intentionally hits a few pain points: very long context, sustained high TPS, and streaming backpressure/timeouts.
[00:25] Liam: We want to be realistic — show where things break and how our platform handles it, not just happy paths.
[00:30] Nina: Perfect. Our main concern is that our product needs to index multi-document conversations (20k tokens) and then serve 500-1k TPS during peak. Also strict SLOs for p95 latency.
[00:42] Carlos: We'll likely try both hosted and dedicated, maybe private later.
[00:45] Priya: Great, so we'll demo three things: API behavior under long context, Console telemetry + Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization, and streaming behavior (how backpressure and timeouts surface and what to do).
[00:58] Liam: Quick note on environment: demo run is against a sandbox cluster, not production. We'll show a small load run, and then screenshots of larger benchmarks from our lab.
[01:06] Nina: Sounds good. Ready when you are.
---
[01:15] Priya: Starting with the Console — here's the per-route dashboard. You can see token breakdown, p50/p95/p99 latencies. If we switch to a profile with very long contexts (24k tokens), you see memory and KV cache heatmaps spike.
[01:32] Priya: (screen) Notice the kernel selection panel. For long context we pick kernels optimized for attention with streaming KV cache, and we also enable quantization profiles when appropriate.
[01:42] Carlos: Quick question — with long context, is it whole sequence in memory or do you do prefix KV caching?
[01:47] Priya: We do prefix KV caching. The runtime keeps a KV cache per session up to configured limits. For extremely long contexts we stream KV segments and evict old prefixes; that reduces activation GPU memory but adds some chunking and re-compute overhead.
[02:02] Samir: Do you expose eviction policies? We need sticky context for some users.
[02:06] Priya: Yes — per-model policy: LRU, time-based TTL, or pin by session ID. You can also tune max KV size per session in the config.
[02:15] Nina: How does that impact latency? If we pin a 20k token KV, p95 will spike right?
[02:20] Priya: Correct — pinned long KV increases memory footprint and increases p95. In our lab benchmarks we saw p95 jump by ~2-4x for certain model sizes when serving pinned 20k vs windowed 4k. We can show numbers.
---
[02:38] Priya: Moving to high TPS: here's our routing and batching controls. For hosted customers we auto-batch with dynamic batch sizes based on queue depth and SLO. For Dedicated you can set fixed max batch to achieve predictable throughput.
[02:53] Carlos: For the 1k TPS case, what's the best practice: increase batch size or decrease batch latency threshold?
[02:58] Priya: It's a balance. Larger batch sizes give better GPU throughput and unit cost, but increase tail latency. Our Optimize tool will recommend a batch size and latency cutoff per route based on your workload. For low-latency SLOs we recommend smaller max-batch with autoscale to more replicas or dedicated capacity.
[03:14] Liam: Also, we can route latency-sensitive traffic to smaller models or quantized variants and route cost-tolerant requests to larger models as a fallback.
[03:22] Nina: Do you support automatic fallback to a different model on timeout?
[03:25] Priya: Yes — routing policies let you fallback to compatible variants. You can configure immediate fallback or a delayed retry.
---
[03:36] Priya: Now demo time: I'll run a simulated long-context + high TPS test. Starting the load generator... note the timestamps.
[03:45] (sound of typing)
[03:50] Priya: Starting 200 TPS sustained for 2 minutes against a model with 12k context window.
[03:55] (graph updates)
[04:00] Priya: You can see queue depth rising briefly, then autoscaling triggers a new worker. Token throughput increases. P95 stays under our configured SLO for this profile (400ms) for most requests, but we do see spikes when KV eviction causes re-compute.
[04:18] Carlos: I see a few timeouts in the stream logs?
[04:21] Priya: Right — we instrument both server side and streaming layer. There are two kinds of timeouts: pipeline timeouts (inference exceeded server timeout) and streaming timeouts (client-side read deadlines). The sandbox client has a 30s read timeout by default which sometimes triggers if the model is generating long responses or if backpressure causes chunked sends.
[04:39] Samir: Can clients get partial responses if the stream times out?
[04:42] Priya: Yes — if a stream times out mid-generation the server will close the stream but the partial tokens sent are still usable. We also support resumable generation for some models where you can re-issue a request starting from the last token. There's a small replay cost because of recompute.
[04:56] Nina: Are you exposing chunked streaming backpressure metrics?
[05:00] Priya: Yes — Console shows streaming RTT, send/receive buffer stats, and per-connection backpressure events. We log client-side disconnects and reason codes.
---
[05:12] Liam: I want to highlight Optimize suggestions shown here: it looked at the traffic profile and suggested quantizing the model to int8 and enabling prefix caching with a 6k pinned window for VIP sessions. That reduced cost per token by 38% in our bench while keeping p95 within 1.3x baseline.
[05:31] Carlos: Did the quantize path change accuracy? Any RMSE or rouge diffs?
[05:36] Priya: Small quality delta for the tasks we tested — we flagged regression to dev tests and we have a rollback policy. Optimize will tie quantization to prompt sets and run evals against your golden prompts before recommending rollout.
[05:49] Carlos: Good.
---
[05:55] Priya: Now switching to streaming backpressure. I'm going to throttle the client read rate to emulate slow consumers.
[06:02] (throttled stream starts)
[06:05] Priya: The server detects backpressure when the TCP send buffer fills or the gRPC stream window stalls. We have a couple responses: 1) buffer and slow the generator (apply token pacing), 2) drop to a lower complexity decoding (e.g., reduce sampling steps), or 3) close the stream with explicit backpressure reason so the client can retry.
[06:25] Samir: Token pacing — is that deterministic? We have real-time UX that needs steady token flow.
[06:29] Priya: We implement token pacing heuristics; it's not perfectly deterministic. For hard real-time UX needs we recommend smaller generation size per request and using streaming keepalive heartbeats. Also, model warmup improves consistency.
[06:42] Nina: What about client-side retry semantics? We don't want duplicated actions.
[06:46] Priya: We recommend idempotency keys for actions that cause side effects. For pure text generation, re-issuing is usually fine but you might get non-deterministic output. We support response signatures and lineage metadata so you can detect duplicates.
---
[06:58] Priya: I'm going to run a high TPS sustained test now: 800 TPS with short seq lengths to show throughput limits and how server-side queueing behaves.
[07:05] (load generator spike)
[07:10] Priya: As expected, batch sizes increase and GPU utilization goes high. If you look at per-CPU network saturations, you can see a small amount of packet queuing — which can translate to small p99 blips. That's where dedicated capacity with multiple replicas or shard-level routing helps.
[07:28] Carlos: For 800 TPS do you recommend Dedicated?
[07:31] Priya: For predictable p95 at that scale, yes. Dedicated reserved pools give you more control: you can pin instance types, pre-warm KV, and get an SLA. Hosted works for bursts but may have more variance.
[07:42] Nina: Any numbers on tokens/sec per GPU for our model family?
[07:46] Priya: For the 70B class we saw ~1.2-1.8k tokens/sec per A100-like GPU with mixed precision; with int8 quantization it can be 2x in some cases depending on sequence length. We'll send a model-specific bench table.
---
[07:58] (minor crosstalk)
[08:03] Carlos: You mentioned autoscale — how fast can autoscale react to sudden load?
[08:06] Liam: Autoscale is policy-driven. Cold start includes model load time and KV warmup — typically 30-90s depending on model and instance. We mitigate with warm pools and predictive scaling. For sudden spikes, we recommend a small buffer of reserved replicas.
[08:20] Samir: If we go private/VPC, do you still recommend warm pools?
[08:23] Priya: Yes; warm pools are available for Private and Dedicated. For private on-prem we can coordinate warm VM images to reduce startup.
---
[08:30] Priya: Let's talk about timeouts and observable signals. When a client sees a timeout, Console surfaces: server timeout hit, stream stall, high GPU mem pressure, or network disconnect. Each has a suggested remediation and links to docs.
[08:45] Nina: We're curious about end-to-end debugging — we need traceability for audits.
[08:49] Priya: We provide request-level traces, token-level timestamps, and audit logs. For Private deployments we can integrate with your ELK stack or Splunk and forward logs via secure channels.
[08:59] Carlos: Does audit include prompt contents? We have PII concerns.
[09:03] Priya: By default we store prompts for a configurable retention period; you can disable retention, redact, or use customer-managed KMS and HSM. We have SOC 2 controls and can provide detailed PCI/SOC2 artifacts.
---
[09:18] Priya: Now a short demo showing a streaming timeout scenario: I'll artificially set server-side inference timeout to 5s and generate a 10s response to show how the client sees partial tokens and error code.
[09:28] (demo)
[09:33] Priya: The stream closed with code BACKPRESSURE_TIMEOUT and partial output contains metadata: session id, lastTokenIndex: 124. You can re-issue starting at token 125.
[09:42] Samir: The ability to resume is valuable, what's the replay cost?
[09:46] Priya: Replay requires reconstructing the KV up to that point; cost depends on pinned vs windowed state. Typical extra cost is 0.5-1x the remaining generation.
[09:55] Nina: If we have webhooks that act on first token, duplication could be an issue.
[09:59] Priya: For webhook-side effects we recommend acknowledging only when stream completes, or using idempotency tokens and lineage metadata.
---
[10:08] Carlos: On the security front, we need SSO, fine-grained RBAC, and audit logs forwarded.
[10:13] Liam: We support SAML SSO, OIDC, SCIM provisioning, fine-grained roles, and audit forwarding. For Private we can integrate with customer KMS.
[10:21] Nina: Also need data residency — EU only for certain workloads.
[10:24] Priya: We can pin region and tenant routing so EU traffic stays in EU zones; for Private on-prem that's native.
---
[10:33] Priya: Wrapping up — lessons from the demo: long context is feasible but requires tradeoffs: pinning for UX vs memory for latency; batching for cost vs tail latency; streaming needs explicit retry/heartbeat patterns for resiliency.
[10:47] Liam: Recap of recommended POC: 1) 48-hour run: simulate our traffic profile (Carlos supplies). 2) Two model variants: quantized and baseline. 3) Run both hosted sandbox then Dedicated POC with 2 reserved nodes. 4) We'll provide bench spreadsheet, runbook, and security docs.
[11:05] Nina: That works. Couple of asks: show detailed p99 numbers, and a breakdown of cost impact of quantization vs added replicas.
[11:12] Liam: We'll include that in the bench sheet.
[11:14] Samir: Also need network diagrams and port/IP requirements for VPC peering.
[11:18] Priya: We'll attach our network checklist and sample terraform for peering.
---
[11:25] Nina: A few quick clarifications: are there any hidden ceilings (like max sessions) with very long pinned contexts?
[11:31] Priya: We enforce per-tenant memory quotas. Very long pinned sessions count heavily. With Dedicated, quotas are higher and configurable. For extreme cases we recommend hybrid approach: ephemeral pinned sessions for VIP users, and shorter windows for general users.
[11:45] Carlos: Any known issues with model families we use (open70b variant)?
[11:49] Priya: For open70b we saw increased memory pressure at 16k+ contexts on older kernels; newer kernels and int8 path mitigate this. We'll document model-specific notes.
---
[12:00] Liam: Okay, next steps recap: we'll send bench spreadsheet and pricing (Liam), Priya will provision load script and sample configs, Carlos will give traffic profile, Samir will send VPC security checklist.
[12:10] Nina: Who should we loop into the VPC discussion?
[12:12] Liam: Our infra specialist, Jordan Lee, will join the deep-dive. We'll schedule for the week of 6/22.
[12:18] Priya: Anything else?
[12:20] Nina: No, that's all. Thanks for the candid demo.
[12:23] Liam: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials.
[12:26] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings — e.g., SOC2 transcribed at times as 'SOC two', KV cache sometimes appears as 'K-V cache'. References to shared artifacts: bench spreadsheet (link: internal/redwood/benchmarks/DSI-2026), network checklist (link: internal/redwood/network-checks/vpc-peering.pdf), security pack (link: internal/redwood/security/soc2-2025.pdf).
